source.title: Signal-Noise Factorization Isolates Nuisance Variation into Removable Subspaces

record.tranche_reason: The study directly manipulates representation regularization and measures held-out performance, but it does not test the claim versions’ specified interventions or measures.
record.gate_note: No mapped version is tested. The study reports held-out performance under SNF and SSF regularization, which is relevant to the broader claim about regularization and generalization; OOD corruption and subspace-projection results are outside the claim’s stated scope.
record.test_reason: The study tests SNF and SSF activation regularizers, which none of V1–V8 names. It reports no random-label comparison, width sweep, architecture comparison, optimizer comparison, batch-size comparison, dropout intervention, magnitude-aware sharpness measure, or memorized-example removal. Its own generalization results therefore test none of the supplied versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that SNF improves performance especially under distribution shift by separating nuisance variation from signal directions, while SSF offers no consistent benefit. They also show that projecting out a validation-estimated nuisance subspace improves corrupted-test accuracy. Their claim of no measurable clean-accuracy cost should be read alongside the lower SNF point estimate and absence of formal statistical tests.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains ResNet-18 classifiers with explicit SNF or SSF activation regularizers, alongside L2 and unregularized baselines; it does not use the claim versions’ interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Regularizer choice changes results: SNF improves held-out CIFAR-100 accuracy and corrupted BloodMNIST accuracy, while SSF lowers CIFAR-100 accuracy and tracks or falls below the L2 baseline under corruption. Corruption severity and type also vary, but those tests are out of scope for the claim.

fits_no_version.finding: On CIFAR-100, SNF improves held-out accuracy over no regularization, and L2+SNF performs best among tested conditions; SSF lowers accuracy relative to corresponding baselines.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Targeted signal-noise regularization can improve held-out accuracy in the tested ResNet-18 setting, whereas signal-signal regularization need not.

fits_no_version.finding: Clean BloodMNIST accuracies are 97.81±0.04% for L2, 97.84±0.24% for L2+SSF, and 97.43±0.13% for L2+SNF. Corruption-averaged accuracies are 57.93±0.96%, 57.27±0.91%, and 61.03±0.83%, respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SNF improves average robustness to the tested BloodMNIST corruptions. The clean-test point estimate is lower than L2's; equivalence or absence of a clean-accuracy cost is not established by a formal test.

record.code_released: Code to reproduce experiments and figures is stated to be on GitHub, with the link to be added upon acceptance/rejection; no URL stated.
record.problems: Only one architecture and two datasets; three random seeds; no formal statistical tests. CIFAR-100 held-out accuracy comparisons are described without exact numerical values in the supplied text. No training error is reported, so train-test gaps cannot be assessed.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from in-scope same-distribution held-out performance results. Corruption robustness and subspace-projection results were not extracted as rows because the claim explicitly separates out-of-distribution generalization.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out performance.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under matched epoch budgets and recipe adaptations; using a scaled learning rate at one batch size supplies no comparison.
Dropout effects, dependence on training-set size or dropout strength, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness, its association with train-test gaps, and ranking against other generalization measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Representation factorization is distinct from magnitude-aware weight sharpness in V7. References to original sources and adoption of learning-rate scaling do not constitute tests of their claims. No additional results bearing on V1–V8 were found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label generalization.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison of measures tracking the train-test gap.
